title: Kesavananda Bharati Sripadagalvaru vs. State of Kerala
presidingJudges: Chief Justice S.M. Sikri, Justice J.M. Shelat, Justice K.S. Hegde, Justice A.N. Grover, Justice H.R. Khanna
respondent: State of Kerala & Union of India
factsSynopsis: The petitioner challenged state enactments restricting the management of religious property. While proceedings were pending, Parliament enacted the 24th, 25th, and 29th Constitutional Amendments curtailing fundamental rights under Articles 14, 19, and 31 and placing state laws into the Ninth Schedule. The petitioner challenged the scope of Parliament's amending power under Article 368.
legalIssues: Whether Parliament's power to amend the Constitution under Article 368 is unlimited, or whether there exist inherent structural limitations protecting the basic framework of the Constitution.
statutesCited: Article 368, Article 13, Article 14, Article 19, Article 31 Constitution of India
precedentsCited: Golak Nath v. State of Punjab (1967) 2 SCR 762; Shankari Prasad v. Union of India (1951)
ratioDecidendi: Parliament has wide power to amend any provision of the Constitution under Article 368, but this power does not extend to altering, damaging, or destroying the Basic Structure of the Constitution. Judicial review and fundamental rights form immutable pillars of the basic structure.
sentenceOrDamages: Basic Structure Doctrine Formulated; 25th Amendment § 3 Struck Down
keyTags: Basic Structure Doctrine, Article 368, Judicial Review, Constitutional Amendments, Fundamental Rights

title: Justice K.S. Puttaswamy (Retd.) vs. Union of India
presidingJudges: Chief Justice J.S. Khehar, Justice J. Chelameswar, Justice S.A. Bobde, Justice D.Y. Chandrachud, Justice R.F. Nariman
petitioner: Justice K.S. Puttaswamy (Former High Court Judge)
respondent: Union of India & Unique Identification Authority of India (UIDAI)
factsSynopsis: A retired High Court judge challenged the mandatory biometric identity scheme. The Union Government contended that the Indian Constitution does not explicitly guarantee an independent fundamental right to privacy.
legalIssues: Whether the right to privacy is a fundamental right guaranteed under Part III of the Constitution of India, intrinsically linked to the right to life and personal liberty under Article 21.
statutesCited: Article 21, Article 19, Article 14 Constitution of India, Aadhaar Act 2016
precedentsCited: M.P. Sharma v. Satish Chandra (1954); Kharak Singh v. State of U.P. (1964); Maneka Gandhi v. Union of India (1978)
ratioDecidendi: The Right to Privacy is a fundamental and inalienable right protected as an intrinsic part of the right to life and personal liberty under Article 21. Any state intrusion into privacy must strictly satisfy the 3-fold proportionality test: legality, legitimate state aim, and proportionality.
sentenceOrDamages: Unanimous Declaration of Fundamental Right to Privacy; Proportionality Standard Mandated
keyTags: Right to Privacy, Article 21, Biometrics, Informational Privacy, Proportionality Standard

title: National Insurance Co. Ltd. vs. Pranay Sethi & Ors.
presidingJudges: Chief Justice Dipak Misra, Justice A.K. Sikri, Justice A.M. Khanwilkar, Justice D.Y. Chandrachud, Justice Ashok Bhushan
respondent: Pranay Sethi & Legal Representatives of Accident Victims
factsSynopsis: Multiple appeals by insurance companies and motor accident claimants regarding standard guidelines for calculating vehicular accident damages, comprehensive property/vehicle loss, and third-party insurance compensation under Sections 166 and 168 of the Motor Vehicles Act.
legalIssues: Standardization of vehicle accident compensation, future economic loss, vehicular damages, and statutory insurance liability under the Motor Vehicles Act 1988.
statutesCited: Motor Vehicles Act 1988 § 166, § 168, § 149 (Insurance Repudiation), Law of Torts
precedentsCited: Sarla Verma v. DTC (2009) 6 SCC 121; Reshma Kumari v. Madan Mohan (2013) 9 SCC 65
ratioDecidendi: Insurance companies are strictly liable to indemnify vehicular damage and accident claims under valid policies. Established uniform standardized heads of compensation for vehicular collision claims, non-pecuniary losses, and standard percentage increases for future economic losses.
sentenceOrDamages: Comprehensive Standardized Vehicular Accident Guidelines Mandated for All Insurers
keyTags: Vehicle Damage, Motor Insurance, Accident Compensation, Motor Vehicles Act § 166, Third Party Liability

title: Sarla Verma & Ors. vs. Delhi Transport Corporation
presidingJudges: Justice R.V. Raveendran, Justice Lokeshwar Singh Panta
respondent: Delhi Transport Corporation & United India Insurance Co.
factsSynopsis: A speeding commercial bus collided with a private vehicle, causing total vehicle destruction and fatal injuries. The insurance corporation contested liability pleading contributory negligence and disputes over vehicle valuation and depreciation formulas.
legalIssues: Determination of just compensation for vehicular destruction, multiplier formula for loss of dependency, and extent of insurer indemnification for commercial transport collisions.
statutesCited: Motor Vehicles Act 1988 § 166, Fatal Accidents Act 1855, Law of Torts Negligence
precedentsCited: General Manager Kerala SRTC v. Susamma Thomas (1994) 2 SCC 176; U.P. SRTC v. Trilok Chandra (1996)
ratioDecidendi: Formulated the definitive standardized multiplier table for motor accident compensation. An insurer cannot avoid liability for vehicular damage where primary driver negligence is established by eye-witness testimony and police collision investigation reports.
sentenceOrDamages: Enhanced Compensation of ₹18,48,000 Awarded with 7.5% Interest from Date of Filing
keyTags: Vehicle Damage, Motor Accident Claims, Insurance Repudiation, Negligence, Multiplier Method

title: Bhuwan Singh vs. Oriental Insurance Company Ltd.
presidingJudges: Justice U.U. Lalit, Justice Vineet Saran
factsSynopsis: The appellant's commercial vehicle met with an accident causing catastrophic damage. The insurance company repudiated the own-damage claim alleging delay of 48 hours in formal written intimation and technical disputes over surveyor assessment of salvage value.
legalIssues: Whether mechanical delays in notifying an insurer or disputes over garage repair estimates justify total repudiation of a genuine vehicle damage insurance claim.
statutesCited: Insurance Act 1938, Consumer Protection Act 1986, Motor Vehicles Act 1988
precedentsCited: Gurshinder Singh v. Shriram General Insurance Co. (2020) 11 SCC 612; Om Prakash v. Reliance General Insurance (2017)
ratioDecidendi: Technical or procedural delay in notifying an insurance company does not warrant repudiation of a genuine vehicle damage claim when the occurrence of the collision is established by police GD entry and surveyor inspection. The insurer must indemnify actual repair costs less standard depreciation.
sentenceOrDamages: Repudiation Set Aside; Insurer Ordered to Pay Full Assessed Repair Costs + 9% Interest
keyTags: Vehicle Damage Claim, Own Damage Insurance, Repudiation of Claim, Surveyor Assessment, Repair Costs

title: Oil & Natural Gas Corporation Ltd. vs. Saw Pipes Ltd.
presidingJudges: Justice M.B. Shah, Justice Arun Kumar
factsSynopsis: ONGC placed an order for casing pipes with Saw Pipes. Due to nationwide labor strikes in Europe, delivery was delayed. ONGC made payments after deducting liquidated damages as specified in the agreed contractual delay clause. Saw Pipes challenged the deduction arguing ONGC suffered no actual proven financial loss.
legalIssues: Whether a party to a commercial contract is entitled to recover agreed liquidated damages under Section 74 of the Contract Act without proving the exact quantum of actual financial loss.
statutesCited: Section 73, Section 74 Indian Contract Act 1872, Arbitration and Conciliation Act 1996 § 34
precedentsCited: Fateh Chand v. Balkishan Dass (1964) 1 SCR 515; Maula Bux v. Union of India (1969) 2 SCC 554
ratioDecidendi: Where terms of a commercial contract clearly stipulate liquidated damages as a genuine pre-estimate of loss, the party complaining of breach is entitled to receive reasonable compensation up to the agreed amount without being required to prove actual loss.
sentenceOrDamages: Arbitral Award Setting Aside Liquidated Damages Overturned; Contractual Deduction Upheld
keyTags: Breach of Contract, Liquidated Damages, Section 74 Contract Act, Commercial Contracts, Public Policy

title: Hadley vs. Baxendale
factsSynopsis: A broken crankshaft stopped operations at the plaintiffs' steam-driven flour mill. Plaintiffs engaged the defendant carrier to transport the broken shaft to the engine maker as a pattern for a replacement. Carrier delayed delivery by several days due to negligence, causing the mill to remain idle and lose £300 in profits.
legalIssues: What is the rule governing remoteness of damages and recoverable compensation for breach of commercial contract.
statutesCited: Common Law of Contracts, Principle of Foreseeability and Consequential Damages
ratioDecidendi: Damages for breach of contract are recoverable under two limbs: (1) damages arising naturally according to the usual course of things, or (2) damages reasonably supposed to have been in the contemplation of both parties at the time the contract was made as the probable result of the breach.
sentenceOrDamages: Special Consequential Damages of Lost Mill Profits Denied; Rule on Foreseeability Established
keyTags: Breach of Contract, Remoteness of Damages, Consequential Damages, Foreseeability, Commercial Law

title: Indian Medical Association vs. V.P. Shantha & Ors.
presidingJudges: Justice S.C. Agrawal, Justice S. Mohan, Justice B.L. Hansaria
factsSynopsis: Medical association contended that medical treatment by doctors and hospitals does not fall within the definition of 'service' under Section 2(1)(o) of the Consumer Protection Act, 1986, and that claims of medical negligence cannot be entertained by consumer forums.
legalIssues: Whether medical professionals and hospitals providing diagnostic and surgical services for consideration fall within the ambit of the Consumer Protection Act.
statutesCited: Consumer Protection Act 1986 § 2(1)(o), § 14, Law of Torts Medical Negligence
precedentsCited: Bolam v. Friern Hospital Management Committee [1957] 1 WLR 582
ratioDecidendi: Medical services rendered by doctors and private hospitals for consideration fall squarely within the definition of 'service' under the Consumer Protection Act. Patients are consumers entitled to claim damages for deficiency in service and medical malpractice before consumer tribunals.
sentenceOrDamages: Medical Profession Brought Under Consumer Protection Jurisdiction; Remedies Affirmed
keyTags: Consumer Protection, Medical Negligence, Deficiency in Service, Professional Liability, Tort Law

title: Google LLC vs. Oracle America, Inc.
courtName: Supreme Court of the United States
presidingJudges: Justice Stephen Breyer (Majority), Justice Clarence Thomas (Dissent)
factsSynopsis: Google copied approximately 11,500 lines of declaring code from 37 Java SE API packages to create the Android mobile operating system, enabling programmers familiar with Java to write applications for Android. Oracle sued Google for billions in copyright damages for verbatim copying of API declarations.
legalIssues: Whether reimplementing software API declaring code for mobile software interoperability constitutes statutory Fair Use under Section 107 of the Copyright Act.
precedentsCited: Campbell v. Acuff-Rose Music, 510 U.S. 569 (1994); Lotus Development Corp. v. Borland (1996)
ratioDecidendi: Google's copying of the Java SE declaring code was a fair use as a matter of law. Reimplementation included only what was necessary to allow programmers to utilize their accumulated knowledge in a new and transformative smartphone environment.
sentenceOrDamages: Fair Use Upheld as Matter of Law; $9 Billion Copyright Claim Dismissed
keyTags: Software Copyright, API Declaring Code, Interoperability, Fair Use, Android

title: Andy Warhol Foundation for the Visual Arts, Inc. vs. Goldsmith
courtName: Supreme Court of the United States
presidingJudges: Justice Sonia Sotomayor (Majority), Chief Justice John Roberts, Justice Elena Kagan (Dissent)
petitioner: Andy Warhol Foundation for the Visual Arts, Inc.
factsSynopsis: Photographer Lynn Goldsmith licensed a portrait of Prince to Vanity Fair for an artist reference. Andy Warhol created a silkscreen based on the photo. Decades later, the Warhol Foundation licensed the silkscreen image to Condé Nast for $10,000 without Goldsmith's permission. The Foundation claimed Fair Use under Copyright Act § 107.
legalIssues: Whether the first fair use factor favors an artist foundation when both the original photograph and secondary artwork are licensed for commercial magazine publications.
statutesCited: 17 U.S. Code § 106, 17 U.S. Code § 107 (Fair Use Factors)
precedentsCited: Campbell v. Acuff-Rose Music, Inc., 510 U.S. 569 (1994)
ratioDecidendi: Under the first fair use factor, commercial licensing of a secondary work to illustrate a magazine article sharing the same commercial purpose as the original work does not constitute transformative fair use.
sentenceOrDamages: Fair Use Defense Rejected; Commercial Licensing Infringement Affirmed
keyTags: Copyright, Fair Use, Transformative Work, First Factor, Licensing

title: Uber BV and Others vs. Aslam and Others
courtName: Supreme Court of the United Kingdom
presidingJudges: Lord Leggatt, Lord Reed, Lady Hale, Lord Hodge, Lady Arden
petitioner: Uber BV, Uber London Ltd & Uber Britannia Ltd
respondent: Yaseen Aslam, James Farrar & Uber Drivers Union
factsSynopsis: Rideshare drivers operating on the Uber platform claimed statutory national minimum wage and paid leave. Uber argued that drivers were independent self-employed contractors with Uber acting solely as a booking software agent.
legalIssues: Whether gig economy app-based rideshare drivers are 'workers' under employment law based on statutory reality rather than contractual labels.
statutesCited: Employment Rights Act 1996 § 230(3)(b), National Minimum Wage Act 1998
ratioDecidendi: Employment classification is determined by reference to statutory purpose and actual subordination. Because Uber exercises extensive algorithmic control over pricing, ratings, and ride allocations, drivers are statutory workers.
sentenceOrDamages: Driver Worker Status Affirmed; Minimum Wage and Holiday Pay Mandated
keyTags: Gig Economy, Worker Status, Algorithmic Control, Minimum Wage, Employment Rights

title: M.C. Mehta vs. Union of India (Oleum Gas Leak Case)
presidingJudges: Chief Justice P.N. Bhagwati, Justice Ranganath Misra, Justice G.L. Oza
respondent: Union of India & Shriram Foods & Fertilizer Industries
factsSynopsis: A catastrophic leak of hazardous oleum gas occurred at the Shriram fertilizer plant in New Delhi, killing an advocate and causing serious respiratory distress to thousands of residents. The company sought to evade strict liability under Rylands v. Fletcher exceptions.
legalIssues: Whether an industrial enterprise engaged in hazardous or inherently dangerous activities is subject to Absolute Liability without exceptions.
statutesCited: Article 21, Article 32 Constitution of India, Water & Air Pollution Control Acts
ratioDecidendi: An enterprise engaged in hazardous industry owes an absolute and non-delegable duty to the community. If harm results, the enterprise is absolutely liable to compensate all affected parties without any common law defenses.
sentenceOrDamages: Doctrine of Absolute Liability Established; Mandatory Compensation Fund Mandated
keyTags: Absolute Liability, Hazardous Industry, Polluter Pays, Article 21, Industrial Disaster

title: Bachan Singh vs. State of Punjab
presidingJudges: Chief Justice Y.V. Chandrachud, Justice A.C. Gupta, Justice P.N. Bhagwati (Dissent)
factsSynopsis: The appellant was convicted of murder under Section 302 IPC and sentenced to death. The appellant challenged the constitutional validity of capital punishment under Section 302 IPC read with Section 354(3) CrPC.
legalIssues: Whether capital punishment violates fundamental rights under Articles 14, 19, and 21, and what judicial standards govern death penalty sentencing discretion.
statutesCited: Section 302 Indian Penal Code, Section 354(3) Code of Criminal Procedure 1973, Article 21 Constitution
precedentsCited: Jagmohan Singh v. State of U.P. (1973) 1 SCC 20
ratioDecidendi: The death penalty does not violate Article 14 or 21 if awarded under a fair procedure. However, capital punishment must be restricted strictly to the 'Rarest of Rare cases' where alternative sentencing is unquestionably foreclosed.
sentenceOrDamages: Death Sentence Commuted; 'Rarest of Rare' Doctrine Formulated
keyTags: Death Penalty, Rarest of Rare, Section 302 IPC, Section 354(3) CrPC, Sentencing Discretion

title: Shreya Singhal vs. Union of India
presidingJudges: Justice J. Chelameswar, Justice Rohinton Fali Nariman
petitioner: Shreya Singhal (Law Student & Free Speech Advocates)
respondent: Union of India (Ministry of Communications and IT)
factsSynopsis: Police arrested two young women under Section 66A of the IT Act for posting online commentary. Petitions challenged the vague and overbroad statutory language of Section 66A, which criminalized sending 'offensive' electronic messages.
legalIssues: Whether Section 66A of the IT Act violates the fundamental right to freedom of speech and expression guaranteed under Article 19(1)(a).
statutesCited: Section 66A, Section 69A, Section 79 Information Technology Act 2000, Article 19(1)(a)
precedentsCited: Romesh Thappar v. State of Madras (1950); Brandenburg v. Ohio (1969)
ratioDecidendi: Section 66A of the IT Act is unconstitutional in its entirety. The provision creates a chilling effect on legitimate free speech and is not saved by reasonable restrictions under Article 19(2).
sentenceOrDamages: Section 66A IT Act Struck Down; Intermediary Safe Harbor Upheld
keyTags: Section 66A IT Act, Free Speech Online, Article 19(1)(a), Chilling Effect, Intermediary Liability
